items.summary: Peppermint oil may have a surprisingly powerful effect on blood pressure. In a randomized study of 40 adults, researchers found that taking small doses twice daily for 20 days lowered systolic blood pressure by an average of 8.5 mmHg. Those receiving a placebo experienced no significant improvement. The discovery points to a promising, low-cost natural approach to managing mildly elevated blood pressure.

The icy object is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and follows an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.

items.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
items.summary: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.

items.title: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
items.summary: A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought. Their findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human-like consciousness.

items.title: Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety
items.summary: An AI-powered analysis of thousands of children's brain scans has revealed three distinct brain types underlying ADHD and anxiety that do not neatly fit traditional diagnoses. These hidden biological patterns can appear before a diagnosis is made, potentially enabling earlier detection and more effective, personalized treatments.

items.title: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity
items.summary: Scientists have successfully transmitted a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity, an old elevator, and an incredibly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, researchers encoded the word "Gravity" into tiny changes in gravitational pull. Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.

items.title: Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang
items.summary: A surprising discovery by MIT and UC Santa Barbara physicists reveals that Einstein’s famous theory of particle motion misses something important when particles travel near the speed of light. Their new calculations show that heavy quarks moving through an ultra-hot plasma experience rare but unusually powerful jolts that Einstein’s traditional model cannot fully explain.

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer
items.summary: A common antibody in the gut may be a powerful natural defense against colon cancer, with researchers finding that mice lacking it developed more than twice as many tumors. Restoring the antibody eliminated the increased risk, revealing a promising new avenue for preventing cancer before it starts.

items.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
items.summary: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.

items.summary: MIT scientists have discovered that tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang could slowly devour stars from within, eventually triggering spectacular explosions visible across galaxies. Detecting these unusual cosmic events could reveal the existence of primordial black holes and help solve the mystery of dark matter.

items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
items.summary: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.

items.title: Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age
items.summary: A major analysis of 149 studies found that cannabis users develop psychosis an average of 2.5 years earlier than non-users, with the difference growing to more than six years among adults 30 and older. Researchers warn that cannabis-related psychiatric risks may accumulate over time, challenging the belief that using marijuana after adolescence is relatively safe.

items.title: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat
items.summary: Researchers have discovered a new subtype of depression that may affect nearly one in four people with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression. Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief.

items.title: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past
items.summary: Scientists studying ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side have uncovered surprising evidence that challenges decades of thinking about the Solar System’s violent past. Instead of a single catastrophic bombardment, asteroid impacts appear to have declined gradually over billions of years, revealing new clues about Earth's early evolution and the origins of life.

items.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

items.title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
items.summary: Earth’s journey from an oxygen-starved world to a planet capable of supporting complex life may have unfolded very differently than scientists once believed. A new analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere in three major stages, with the oceans taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to catch up.

items.title: Depression may be an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease
items.summary: Depression in older adults may be more than a mental health concern. Scientists discovered that accumulating tau protein, a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, was linked to worsening depressive symptoms in people who still had normal memory and thinking abilities. The faster tau built up in the brain, the faster depressive symptoms increased, suggesting that mood changes could emerge before cognitive decline.

items.title: New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good
items.summary: Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative gum disease treatment that uses egg yolk antibodies and near-infrared light to destroy harmful bacteria without harming beneficial microbes. Unlike conventional treatments, the approach preserves the mouth's natural bacterial balance and protects healthy gum cells. In mice, it significantly reduced the bone loss associated with periodontitis, a major cause of tooth loss.

items.title: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way
items.summary: A surprising discovery suggests the Milky Way may be making stars in places where most galaxies cannot. Scientists found evidence that a massive rotating structure near the galactic center is creating powerful shock waves that trigger star formation rather than suppress it. Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.

items.title: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation
items.summary: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, powered by two enormous black holes that existed just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Weighing an astonishing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants somehow grew to incredible sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.

items.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
items.summary: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.

items.title: Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis
items.summary: A groundbreaking study reveals that acute myeloid leukemia (AML), an aggressive blood cancer, can begin developing more than 50 years before diagnosis, with the first cancer-driving mutation appearing before age 20 in two-thirds of cases. Scientists discovered that these mutated cells grow in surprisingly predictable patterns, accelerating dramatically as additional mutations accumulate.

items.title: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
items.summary: Scientists have discovered an unusual carbon signature in Hawaiian volcanic rocks that suggests some of Earth's carbon originated in ancient meteorites and later escaped from deep within the planet's core. The discovery raises an astonishing possibility: Carbon essential to life may have traveled from space to Earth's depths before emerging through volcanoes billions of years later.

items.title: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman
items.summary: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.

items.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
items.summary: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.

items.title: Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells
items.summary: Scientists have discovered brain cells that actively generate the irresistible urge to sleep, and shutting them down allowed mice to sleep 70% less than normal. Remarkably, many of the animals avoided the severe behavioral consequences of sleep deprivation, raising intriguing possibilities for future sleep research.

items.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years as vaccine myths persist
items.summary: The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, and a new survey reveals widespread misconceptions about the deadly disease and its vaccine. With measles cases surging, more than one-third of Americans still believe or are uncertain about the debunked vaccine-autism link, while most don't know the disease's risks or how many vaccine doses children need.

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging
items.summary: Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than scientists previously realized, with new research linking lower spinal bone density to faster cognitive decline and accelerated changes in the brain's white matter. The surprising connection suggests that routine medical scans could help uncover hidden warning signs of brain aging and identify people at increased risk of dementia.

items.title: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
items.summary: Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.

items.title: Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds
items.summary: People with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, according to a major new review of 40 studies. Researchers estimate that nearly five out of every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes develop Alzheimer’s each year. By focusing specifically on these two conditions, the study offers a clearer understanding of a potentially serious connection between metabolic health and brain health.

items.title: Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a surprising obstacle to interstellar travel: at extreme speeds, the light propelling futuristic solar sails could actually begin slowing them down. Once a spacecraft reaches 75% of the speed of light, some scattered light starts producing drag, potentially complicating humanity’s plans to reach distant stars.

items.title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
items.summary: Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.

items.title: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.

items.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
items.summary: At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.

items.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
items.summary: Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.

items.title: NASA's Curiosity Mars Rover Collects Samples
items.summary: This collage shows 49 drill holes captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover as of November 2026.

items.title: Lake Pelku
items.summary: Lake Pelku (near center), on the Chinese side of the snow-capped Himalayas with Nepal on the adjacent side, is pictured from the International Space Station as it orbited above Asia.

items.title: Rain breaks up Earth’s natural sunshades
items.summary: EarthCARE sheds light on one of the processes that leads to the breakup of vast, bright clouds that help keep our planet cool – with rain emerging as a key driver.

items.title: Watch live: Hera’s first images of post-impact asteroid Dimorphos
items.summary: A little more than four years ago, humans moved an asteroid, as NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted a body called Dimorphos. Now the European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft has arrived at that same asteroid to find out what happened next. Join the Hera team on the evening of…

items.title: Seven-spacecraft observatory to study plasma universe
items.summary: ESA Member States have selected Plasma Observatory as the agency’s next medium-class mission. Its seven coordinated spacecraft will track how the Sun’s energy moves through Earth’s magnetic shield, across different scales of distance and time.

items.title: Empire State Building Goes Gold for Voyager
items.summary: The Empire State Building is seen illuminated in gold to celebrate NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft as it is about to pass one light-day away from Earth, a distance reached by no other human-made object, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, in New York City.

items.title: First thermal images from Sentinel-3C radiometer
items.summary: These are the first images showing land- and sea-surface temperatures from the third satellite of the Copernicus Sentinel-3 mission, Sentinel-3C.

items.title: In the shadow of volcanic giants
items.summary: Even Mars’s more modest volcanoes demand attention. This month’s snapshot from ESA’s Mars Express spotlights Tharsis Tholus, a fascinating peak with an eventful past.

items.title: Space Selfie
items.summary: NASA astronaut and Expedition 75 flight engineer Anil Menon takes an out-of-this-world “space selfie.”

items.title: Prodex at 40: advancing European space science
items.summary: For forty years, Prodex, the European Space Agency’s Programme for the Development of Scientific Experiments, has turned the scientific ambitions of its Participating States into instruments and experiments flown in space.

items.title: Hera surveying asteroids with superhuman vision
items.summary: The European Space Agency’s Hera mission for planetary defence surveys its target asteroids with a combination of instruments, peering beyond the limits of the human eye. The larger Didymos asteroid – dominated by its dramatic equatorial ridge – is seen here from just 28.5 km…

items.title: Thunderbirds in Formation
items.summary: U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds fighter jets pass overhead during the agency’s MAX POWER expo and air show on Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026, at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

items.title: Outbursts from a Massive Star
items.summary: Using Chandra, astronomers have discovered a previously hidden black hole or neutron star companion that is triggering repeated outbursts from a giant, unstable star.
